prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest combination of original idea, decisive experiment and independent confirmation on the shortlist. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock removed the Doppler and recoil limits while keeping thousands of atoms in the interrogation. Ye's group then drove the systematic uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and added the many-body clock. Many laboratories (RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) reproduce the performance. Intercontinental comparisons and the metrology roadmap towards a new SI second show the result is durable, and it enables tests of constants and relativistic geodesy that were not possible before. This is the kind of new measurement capability I would defend to the Academy as lasting physics. It is also the only candidate where seven of eight members have it ranked, with a two-name credit that every proposer has independently converged on.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize looks like a continuation of the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for trapped-ion control. A sceptic can say the lattice clock is an excellent refinement of metrology rather than a new discovery, and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the practical payoff is still ahead. There is also a real attribution gap: Lemonde, Takamoto and others, and the ion-clock lineage, are outside the credited names, and Ye also appears in other candidacies. The citation must therefore be written around the lattice-clock invention itself and not around clocks in general.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B004 first as precision-meets-theory atomic physics, but warns that Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) may make the committee see clocks as a continuation.
responses.response: I take that overlap seriously and I think the answer is in the citation. The 2005 prize was for the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize for control of single ions. Neither covers neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength, which is Katori's specific idea and what allows thousands of atoms to be interrogated at once. I would resist your suggestion that the redefinition of the second is a precondition. The merit stands on the demonstrated 1e-18 performance across independent labs. I do agree that a redefinition would strengthen the case and that we should check this point with AMO experts, since I rely on you for the priority details.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B004 first as a new measurement technique, and gives B034 (circuit QED) second because it supplied the architecture behind superconducting quantum processors.
responses.response: I share your instrument-builder's view of B004, and I like that you credit Ye with the many-body clock and the comb integration. Where I differ is on B034 as the second candidate. I rank it outside my top choices because the 2025 prize already recognised macroscopic quantum behaviour in superconducting circuits, and I am not convinced circuit QED is distinct enough for the committee to defend, nor am I competent to judge the credit among Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf and Girvin. For a possible second part, I find your atom-interferometry ranking (B036) closer to my own taste, because it too is a measurement technique that has been reproduced and commercialised.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B034 first, arguing that circuit QED is a new quantum-optical platform underlying superconducting processors, while flagging both the 2025 overlap and his own closeness to the field.
responses.response: Thank you for flagging the conflict openly, which I think the committee should note in the record when B034 is discussed. On substance I agree with you that the interpretation is stable and widely reproduced. My concern is exactly the one you raise: after the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits, a second prize so soon in the same hardware family is hard to justify, and the choice of three from four names (Blais or Girvin) looks unresolved even among the people who proposed it. B004 placed third on your own ballot; I would ask whether you see any scientific obstacle to it, as opposed to simply preferring your own field.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B010) first for the theory-to-experiment link, ahead of topological insulators and DMFT, and ranks lattice clocks sixth while deferring to AMO colleagues.
responses.response: I accept the physical case for B010: a quantitative prediction from Bistritzer and MacDonald followed by an experimental surprise, with many groups reproducing it. I ranked it seventh not out of dismissal but because the pairing mechanism is still open and the field is only about eight years old, and the credit leaves out Cao and the early moire theorists. I would be glad to hear from you whether you consider the interpretation settled enough. Because I am outside condensed matter I will defer to you on that. If the committee prefers a two-part prize, I would not want B010 to be crowded out merely because it has five names under three slots.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks baryon acoustic oscillations (B045) first and IceCube (B032) second, valuing cosmological measurements and new observational windows, and notes that source-population claims in neutrino astronomy are premature.
responses.response: We agree on IceCube as a new window, and I rank it second. I also agree with your caution: the diffuse flux is firmly established, but the origin of most of it is unsolved, so I would not make it the centre of this year's prize. On B045 I am more hesitant than you are, because the baryon acoustic ruler is part of a family of dark-energy results already recognised in 2011 and 2019, and the credit would have to separate two survey teams from theorists, one of whom is deceased. I would like you to explain which part of the BAO story you consider the decisive discovery that is not already covered by those prizes.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the optical lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on how the citation is worded.
Priority between Katori's proposal and first demonstration versus the performance records from Ye's group, and the roles of Lemonde, Takamoto and others outside the credited names.
Whether a second part (for example B032 or B036) should be added, or whether a single two-person prize is cleaner.
The redefinition of the SI second has not happened and could change how timely the recognition looks.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B004. For B032 (IceCube) I work in the same astroparticle field and the same community, though I am not in the IceCube collaboration (my collaborations are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur), so I would flag that as an area where I should not be the sole judge; I am not recommending it as the preferred prize. I have no apparent connection to the persons credited on the other shortlisted candidates.
